{
  "question_intent": "Discuss UK corporate loan growth, market backdrop, and tax impact on UK PBT",
  "main_topics": [
    "UK corporate loan growth",
    "Market backdrop",
    "Tax impact on UK PBT"
  ],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": false,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "So just picking back up on UK corporate loan growth, obviously a bit more [broader than] before. Your peer banks have anticipated that they see improved and resilient corporate loan demand, obviously you are having some success. I think 70% loan growth was coming from existing clients. Could you comment a bit further on what you are seeing in the market broadly, do you see the broader market backdrop better than you expected given the acceleration in non-financial corporate loan growth that we see in the Bank of England data? And then on tax, we looked at another few months of uncertainty in the run up to the budget. At the Q1 breakfast, you indicated about £35 million pounds impact per 1% increase in the surcharge. Your last country snapshot showed about five and a half billion of UK profit before tax. Could you help us understand which parts of that UK PBT that I consider non-banking for the purposes of the surcharge calculation and just give us an update?",
  "answer_quote": "Okay, so let me start with corporate loan growth. So I think the start point, if you look at page five [of the Q2 results presentation]. So there has been a de-leveraging from UK corporates, and one might argue that if you took the COVID spike out, that de-leveraging has been slowly, slowly happening since the GFC. And so where we start from as a country is a low loan to GDP ratio, which means that there is the capacity to take on lending within corporates. The same is true of households. And so what we are seeing is somewhat structural demand. Where does that come from? We see it very heavily in technology and there are probably a few things underpinning that. One is the kind of thing that we've discussed here today, the ability to deploy technology more flexibly, more cheaply than before. I want to say about 70% of the corporates that we've surveyed have talked about cyber. You don't have to be a large corporate to have concerns around cyber and therefore we've seen some deployment into there, and clearly around productivity more generally given the increase in the national minimum wage and employers NII, that is clearly front of mind for corporates. So we're seeing that loan demand come through. I wouldn't call out any particular sector or region. It's very, very broad based and if I can move you to, I think it's slide 15. For us, I guess we knew that was a backdrop, as we entered our plan. We also knew two other things. The first was we were starting from a position where we had actively, for a number of years, tried not to lend to our existing corporate book because of the place where it sat. It just did not get the capital or the investment to do so. So we knew that we had a group of clients already within the bank with a cash relationship, which by the way is the hard bit to get, to whom we were not lending. And the second thing is we have been deploying both process change and capability in order to drive and underpin that. So I would say there is clearly a demand and there is clearly a capability build on our part. What I want to do here is also just clarify one point which has been raised, which is, there is an increase in risk taking across corporate lending. For us, that is certainly not true. So if you look at the chart on the bottom left hand corner [on slide 15], that has the distribution of the default grades in it. So if you look on around page 72 of our Pillar 3 [report], you are going to find the default grades, I'll excuse you if you haven't found it up to now, think of that as like a FICO for a corporate. What that chart shows you is that in 2023 and now, the distribution of those default grades is not deteriorating. So in other words, neither the passage of time, the lending that we are doing nor the macroeconomic environment is deteriorating that. Now to be clear, we would not originate at a default grade 22, but sometimes you get migration into that. Think of it a bit like stage migration and impairment. To your point on tax, I stick to the £35 million. PBT of £5 billion in the UK, but do remember there are several things that are going into that tax calculation, that for example, would be below the line. So we would have some of the interest payments below the line on our debt. We would also have deferred tax assets. We also have some index linked gilts, which will give us some protection. So £35 million is the number you should be [looking at]. Thank you. Okay, next question please.",
  "main_topics": [
    "UK corporate loan growth",
    "Market backdrop",
    "Tax impact on UK PBT"
  ],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": false,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "contains_forward_guidance": false
}
